What is an Agent? An agent is an autonomous computational entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon it through actuators to achieve specific goals. Unlike traditional programs that simply execute predetermined instructions, agents are adaptive and intelligent. Key components include: • Sensors - gather information from the environment • Actuators - perform actions that affect the environment • Decision-making system - processes input and selects actions
The Agent-Environment Loop Environment Percepts Sensor Input Agent Decision Actuator Actions

Key Components of an Agent Sensors Input mechanisms that gather information from the environment, ranging from simple temperature readings to complex camera systems and data streams. Decision-Making Unit The cognitive core that processes sensory information, evaluates options, and determines appropriate actions based on goals and current state. Actuators Output mechanisms that execute decisions and perform actions in the environment, from mechanical movements to digital communications.

The Perception-Action Cycle At the heart of every agent lies the fundamental perception-action cycle. The agent continuously observes its environment, processes this information through its internal reasoning mechanisms, and executes actions that modify the environment—creating a feedback loop that enables learning and adaptation. This cycle distinguishes agents from passive software components, making them proactive participants in their environments rather than mere tools awaiting commands.

Four Fundamental Characteristics of Agents Autonomy Operates independently without direct human intervention, making decisions based on internal goals and environmental conditions. Reactivity Responds appropriately and in a timely manner to environmental changes and unexpected situations. Proactiveness Takes initiative to achieve goals, planning and executing actions rather than merely responding to stimuli. Social Ability Communicates and coordinates with other agents or humans using established protocols and languages.

Real-World Agent Example: Self-Driving Car Reactivity Instantly responds to pedestrians, traffic signals, and road conditions using cameras, LIDAR, and radar sensors. Proactiveness Plans optimal routes, anticipates traffic patterns, and makes strategic lane changes to reach destinations efficiently. Social Ability Communicates with other vehicles, traffic infrastructure, and cloud services to share traffic data and coordinate movements. Autonomy Makes independent driving decisions, handles unexpected situations, and operates without constant human oversight.

What are Multi-Agent Systems? A Multi-Agent System (MAS) is a collection of multiple autonomous agents that interact within a shared environment to solve problems that are beyond the capabilities of individual agents. No Central Controller Intelligence and coordination emerge from the interactions between agents rather than top- down control. Distributed Problem-Solving Complex tasks are decomposed and solved collaboratively across multiple specialized agents. Flexible Interaction Agents can cooperate, compete, or negotiate depending on their goals and the system's requirements.

Cooperative vs Competitive MAS Cooperative Systems Agents share common goals and work together to maximize overall system performance. Examples include: • Search and rescue robot teams • Distributed sensor networks • Collaborative filtering systems Competitive Systems Agents pursue individual goals that may conflict with others, requiring strategic thinking and game theory. Examples include: • Algorithmic trading systems • Resource allocation markets • Competitive gaming AI

MAS Applications in Robotics Swarm robotics represents one of the most exciting applications of multi-agent systems. Individual robots with simple capabilities can achieve complex collective behaviors through local interactions and emergent coordination. Search & Rescue Drones coordinate to cover large areas efficiently, sharing information about survivors and hazards. Construction Robot teams collaborate to build structures, each contributing specialized skills and capabilities. Environmental Monitoring Sensor networks collect and analyze environmental data across vast geographic regions.

MAS in Economics and Finance 1 Electronic Auctions Automated bidding agents represent buyers and sellers, optimizing strategies in real-time to maximize utility and minimize costs. 2 Algorithmic Trading High-frequency trading systems execute thousands of transactions per second, analyzing market patterns and competing for profitable opportunities. 3 Supply Chain Management Agents coordinate across suppliers, manufacturers, and retailers to optimize inventory, reduce costs, and improve delivery times.

Healthcare Applications Intelligent Hospital Systems Multi-agent systems transform healthcare delivery by coordinating complex hospital operations, patient care, and resource allocation. Agent-based solutions can: • Optimize staff scheduling across departments • Coordinate patient flow and bed management • Monitor patient vital signs and alert medical staff • Manage medical equipment and supply inventories • Support clinical decision-making with real-time data These systems reduce wait times, improve patient outcomes, and maximize resource utilization while maintaining high standards of care.

Network and Traffic Control Modern network systems rely heavily on multi-agent architectures to manage complexity and ensure optimal performance. In computer networks, routing protocols act as agents that discover paths, balance loads, and adapt to network changes autonomously. Dynamic Routing Network agents continuously update routing tables based on traffic patterns and link availability. Traffic Management Smart traffic systems coordinate signal timing to optimize flow and reduce congestion. Security Monitoring Distributed security agents detect and respond to threats across network infrastructure.

Social Simulation and Modeling Epidemic Modeling Agents represent individuals with different behaviors, health states, and social connections to simulate disease transmission and intervention strategies. Crowd Dynamics Virtual pedestrians with individual goals and behaviors help design safer public spaces and predict emergency evacuation patterns. Market Simulation Economic agents with diverse strategies and preferences model market behavior, bubble formation, and regulatory impacts.

Case Study: Google Maps as MAS The System Every smartphone user becomes an agent, contributing real-time location and speed data. The system aggregates millions of individual data points to create dynamic traffic intelligence. Why Study Agents? Understanding agents and multi-agent systems is crucial for the future of technology. As our world becomes increasingly connected and automated, the principles you'll learn in this course form the foundation for the next generation of intelligent systems.

Future Relevance & Career Impact Core to Modern AI Agent-based approaches are fundamental to artificial intelligence, machine learning systems, and autonomous decision-making technologies that are reshaping industries worldwide. Distributed Computing As systems become more distributed and decentralized, understanding how autonomous components interact becomes essential for building scalable, resilient architectures. Internet of Things (IoT) Billions of connected devices require agent-based coordination and communication protocols to function effectively as cohesive systems.

The Foundation of Autonomous Systems Artificial Intelligence Agents embody AI principles in practical, deployable systems that can reason, learn, and adapt in real-world environments. Distributed Systems Multi-agent architectures provide robust, scalable solutions for distributed computing challenges and fault tolerance. Internet of Things IoT devices increasingly act as intelligent agents, making autonomous decisions and coordinating with other smart devices. These technologies converge to create the autonomous systems that will define the next generation of computing, from smart homes to autonomous factories.

Foundational Technologies Robotics E-commerce Smart Cities Autonomous Vehicles Agent and multi-agent system principles are the building blocks for breakthrough innovations across multiple domains. From autonomous robots working in warehouses to smart city infrastructure coordinating traffic and energy distribution, these technologies rely on the concepts we'll explore throughout this course. Understanding these foundations positions you at the forefront of technological innovation, whether you pursue careers in AI research, robotics engineering, distributed systems design, or emerging fields we haven't yet imagined.

Industry Applications and Career Opportunities Autonomous Vehicles Self-driving cars, delivery robots, and aerial drones all rely on agent-based architectures for navigation and decision-making. Smart Systems From virtual assistants to smart home automation, intelligent agents are becoming ubiquitous in consumer technology. E-Commerce Recommendation systems, price optimization, and supply chain management all leverage multi-agent approaches for competitive advantage. Industry 4.0 Manufacturing systems use agent-based control for flexible production, quality control, and predictive maintenance.

Course Structure Overview This 14-week course is carefully designed to build your understanding progressively, from fundamental concepts to advanced applications and real- world projects. Each phase builds upon previous knowledge while introducing new challenges and practical applications. By the end, you'll have both theoretical understanding and hands-on experience with agent-based systems.

Weeks 1 -2: Agents and Environments Foundation Phase We begin with the fundamental concepts that define intelligent agents and their relationship with their operating environments. Key Topics: • Agent properties and characteristics • Environment types and complexity • Performance measures and rationality • Simple reflex vs. goal-based agents Programming assignment: Implement a simple reactive agent in Python that navigates a grid world environment.

Weeks 3-5: Agent Architectures 1 Week 3: Reactive Architectures Behavior-based systems, subsumption architecture, and real-time response mechanisms for dynamic environments. 2 Week 4: Cognitive Architectures Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) model, planning systems, and reasoning mechanisms for complex goal achievement. 3 Week 5: Hybrid Approaches Layered architectures that combine reactive and deliberative components for robust, adaptable agent behavior. This phase explores the internal designs that enable agents to process information, make decisions, and execute actions effectively in complex environments.

Weeks 6-8: Communication and Interaction Understanding how agents coordinate and collaborate is crucial for building effective multi-agent systems. This phase covers the protocols, languages, and mechanisms that enable meaningful agent interaction. 1 Communication Protocols Message-passing systems, synchronization mechanisms, and distributed coordination protocols for reliable agent communication. 2 Agent Communication Languages FIPA-ACL, ontologies, and semantic understanding for sophisticated inter- agent dialogue and knowledge sharing. 3 Coordination Mechanisms Task allocation, consensus algorithms, and distributed problem-solving techniques for collaborative agent systems.

Weeks 9-1 1 : Game Theory and Decision-Making When agents have competing or conflicting interests, strategic thinking becomes essential. This phase introduces mathematical frameworks for modeling and analyzing agent interactions. Strategic Games Nash equilibria, dominant strategies, and solution concepts for multi-agent decision scenarios. Cooperative Game Theory Coalition formation, Shapley values, and fair allocation mechanisms for collaborative agent systems. Mechanism Design Auction theory, incentive compatibility, and market-based coordination for economic agent interactions. Evolutionary Approaches Population dynamics, evolutionary stable strategies, and adaptive behavior in agent populations.

Agent Properties Autonomy ⚫An agent is a computer system capable of autonomous action in some environment in order to meet its design objectives ⚫Usually the environment is complex and dynamic, and agents should interact with it in real time. o Main property: Autonomous capable of acting independently, exhibiting control over their internal state sens ors A ge nt actu ators E N V I R O N M E N T action perception

Agent Properties Autonomy, Flexibility ⚫Trivial (non-interesting) agents: ◼thermostat ⚫Def. 2: An intelligent agent is a computer system capable of flexible autonomous action in some environment ⚫By flexible, we mean: ◼reactive (response capability) ◼pro-active (taking initiative) ◼social (interacting with others)

Agent Properties Reactivity ⚫If a program’s environment is guaranteed to be fixed, the program need never worry about its own success or failure – program just executes blindly ◼Example of fixed environment: compiler ⚫The real world is not like that: things change, information is incomplete. Many (most?) interesting environments are dynamic ⚫Software is hard to build for dynamic domains: program must take into account possibility of failure – ask itself whether it is worth executing! ⚫A reactive system is one that maintains an ongoing interaction with its environment, and responds to changes that occur in it (in time for the
that maintains an ongoing interaction with its environment, and responds to changes that occur in it (in time for the response to be useful)

Agent Properties Proactiveness ⚫Reacting to an environment is easy (e.g., stimulus → response rules) ⚫But we generally want agents to do things for us ⚫Hence goal directed behavior ⚫Pro-activeness = generating and attempting to achieve goals; not driven solely by events; taking the initiative ⚫Recognizing opportunities

Agent Properties Social Ability ⚫The real world is a multi-agent environment: we cannot go around attempting to achieve goals without taking others into account ⚫Some goals can only be achieved with the cooperation of others ⚫Similarly for many computer environments: witness the Internet ⚫Social ability in agents is the ability to interact with other agents (and possibly humans) via some kind of agent-communication language, and perhaps cooperate with others

Agent Properties Balancing Reactive and Goal-Oriented Behavior ⚫We want our agents to be reactive, responding to changing conditions in an appropriate (timely) fashion ⚫We want our agents to systematically work towards long-term goals ⚫These two considerations can be at odds with one another ⚫Reactivy vs. Deliberation balance ◼Designing an agent that can balance reactivity and deliberation (reason about long term goals) remains an open research problem

Other Agent Properties (desireable, not mandatory) ⚫mobility ◼the ability of an agent to move around an electronic network ⚫veracity ◼an agent will not knowingly communicate false information ⚫benevolence ◼agents do not have conflicting goals, and that every agent will therefore always try to do what is asked of it ⚫rationality ◼agent will act in order to achieve its goals, and will not act in such a way as to prevent its goals being achieved — at least insofar as its beliefs permit ⚫learning/adaption ◼agents improve performance over time
beliefs permit ⚫learning/adaption ◼agents improve performance over time

Environment properties Accessible vs. inaccessible ⚫An accessible environment is one in which the agent can obtain complete, accurate, up-to-date information about the environment’s state ⚫Most moderately complex environments (including, for example, the everyday physical world and the Internet) are inaccessible ⚫The more accessible an environment is, the simpler it is to build agents to operate in it

Environment properties Deterministic vs. non-deterministic ⚫A deterministic environment is one in which any action has a single guaranteed effect — there is no uncertainty about the state that will result from performing an action ⚫The physical world can to all intents and purposes be regarded as non- deterministic ⚫Non-deterministic environments present greater problems for the agent designer

Environment properties Episodic vs. non-episodic ⚫In an episodic environment, the performance of an agent is dependent on a number of discrete episodes, with no link between the performance of an agent in different scenarios ⚫Episodic environments are simpler from the agent developer’s perspective because the agent can decide what action to perform based only on the current episode — it need not reason about the interactions between this and future episodes

Environment properties Static vs. dynamic ⚫A static environment is one that can be assumed to remain unchanged except by the performance of actions by the agent ⚫A dynamic environment is one that has other processes operating on it, and which hence changes in ways beyond the agent’s control ⚫Other processes can interfere with the agent’s actions (as in concurrent systems theory) ⚫The physical world is a highly dynamic environment

Environment properties Discrete vs. continuous ⚫An environment is discrete if there are a fixed, finite number of actions and percepts in it ⚫Russell and Norvig give a chess game as an example of a discrete environment, and taxi driving as an example of a continuous one ⚫Continuous environments have a certain level of mismatch with computer systems ⚫Discrete environments could in principle be handled by a kind of “lookup table”

Agent types Physical (embodied) Agents vs. Software Agents ⚫Software agents’ environment is a virtual one ◼Single machine, intranet, internet ◼Interact with other software agents, with sw modules, services ◼Interact with humans through human interfaces ⚫Physical agents or embodied agents ◼Interact with real world (sensors, actuators connected to real world) ◼Problems of perception and action ◼Best known example: Robots.

Utility Functions over States ⚫A task specification is a function u : E → # which associates a real number with every environment state ⚫But what is the value of a run… ◼minimum utility of state on run? ◼maximum utility of state on run? ◼sum of utilities of states on run? ◼average? ⚫Disadvantage: difficult to specify a long term view when assigning utilities to individual states (One possibility: a discount for states later on.)

Utilities over Runs ⚫Another possibility: assigns a utility not to individual states, but to runs themselves: u : R → # ⚫Such an approach takes an inherently long term view ⚫Other variations: incorporate probabilities of different states emerging ⚫Difficulties with utility-based approaches: ◼where do the numbers come from? ◼we don’t think in terms of utilities! ◼hard to formulate tasks in these terms

LLM-based systems vs. Agentic systems ⚫A Large Language Model (LLM) is the statistical text-generating component, typically a Transformer trained to predict the next token given a context. ⚫In recent practice, however, tasks are rarely solved by an LLM in isolation; solutions are produced by an LLM-based system ◼wraps the model with prompts, control logic, optional memory ◼(in agentic settings) adds tool interfaces. ⚫Agentic AI is a term used in an inconsistent manner, but it tipically refers to systems where: ◼instead of asking the model for a single answer to a query, the system runs the model on multiple queries, with
of asking the model for a single answer to a query, the system runs the model on multiple queries, with intermediate outputs inspected and used to decide what to do next

Agentic Systems vs. Agents ⚫Currently “Agentic AI” term is applied to two different architectures: ◼entirely internal loop: the model drafts, critiques, and revises, or explores multiple candidate lines of reasoning before selecting an answer without inspection/modification of the environment ◼external loop: the loop is based in an environment external to the system: the model queries tools, observes results, and iteratively updates its actions based on feedback from the world

Multiagent Systems’ architecture ⚫Agents in a multiagent system tend to interact through a middleware layer ⚫This middleware provides connectivity between agents, solving low- level connectivity issues, including: ◼Updated environment state (after agents’ actions) ◼Environmental (partial) perception ◼Environmental resource usage ◼Communication methods ⚫In FIPA IEEE standard: this middleware is called agent platform

Social Ability Why agent communication? ⚫In order to solve distributed problems, agents need to coordinate (cooperate, compete) with others. ⚫For this Agents need to communicate ⚫Goals for Agent Communication: ◼Agents able to request (to other ags.) actions or services that they cannot perform by themselves ◼Agents able to ask for information (to other ags.) ◼Agents able to share their beliefs with other ags. ◼Agents able to coordinate with other ags. To solve complex tasks.

Communication methods ⚫Blackboard systems ◼Agents communicate information through a common data structure, accessible by everybody ◼Problem: if there is no middleware to provide some concurrency, it tends to become a bottleneck. ⚫Message passing ◼Agents communicate directly by means of messages ◼The agent platform usually acts as message router ◼Common communication language (e.g. FIPA-ACL) ◼Common communication protocols (message format, steps in a communication)

Levels in Agent Communication ⚫Four levels in communication (FIPA IEEE standard): ◼Message Semantics •What does each message means? •3 components –Message type (performative): gives intensionality –Message content: contains the information –Ontology (the message refers to) ◼Message Sintaxis •How each message is expressed? •2 components –Message structure: Agent Communication Language –Content codification: Content Language ◼Interaction protocol •How are conversations/dialogues structured? –Agent Protocols ◼Transport protocol •How messages are actually sent and received by agents?
